sceneHappening: Saul meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, and Peter heals at Lydda and Joppa
summary: Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, goes to the high priest and asks for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he finds any who belong to the Way, men or women, he may bring them bound to Jerusalem. As he travels and draws near to Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven shines around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" "Who are you, Lord?" "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise up, and enter into the city, and it will be told you what you must do." The men traveling with him stand speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul arises from the ground, and though his eyes are open, he sees nothing, so they lead him by the hand into Damascus. He is three days without sight, and neither eats nor drinks. A disciple named Ananias in Damascus is told by the Lord in a vision, "Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judas for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, and has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight." Ananias objects: "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name." The Lord says, "Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name's sake." Ananias goes, lays his hands on him, and says, "Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, who appeared to you on the way by which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit." Immediately something like scales falls from his eyes and he receives his sight; he rises and is baptized, and when he has taken food he is strengthened. He spends some days with the disciples in Damascus, and immediately proclaims in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. All who hear him are amazed: "Isn't this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name?" But Saul grows more powerful and confounds the Jews who live at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ. After many days the Jews plot to kill him, but their plot becomes known to Saul, and the disciples take him by night and let him down through the wall in a basket. At Jerusalem he tries to join the disciples, but they are all afraid of him, not believing he is a disciple, until Barnabas takes him to the apostles and tells how he had seen the Lord on the road and how in Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. He moves freely among them in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord, and disputes with the Hellenists, who try to kill him; when the brothers learn of it, they bring him to Caesarea and send him off to Tarsus. So the church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria has peace, being built up, and walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, is multiplied. Peter, traveling through all those parts, comes to the saints at Lydda and finds a man named Aeneas, who has been bedridden eight years, paralyzed: "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Arise, and make your bed." He arises immediately, and all who live at Lydda and in Sharon see him and turn to the Lord. In Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which in Greek is Dorcas, is full of good works and acts of mercy, and she falls sick and dies. The disciples, hearing that Peter is nearby, send two men asking him to come without delay. When he arrives he is taken to the upper room, where all the widows stand by him weeping and showing the tunics and garments Dorcas made. Peter sends them out, kneels down and prays, then turns to the body and says, "Tabitha, arise." She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up. He gives her his hand and raises her, calls the saints and widows, and presents her alive. It becomes known throughout all Joppa, and many believe in the Lord. Peter stays many days in Joppa with Simon, a tanner.
whySettingMatters: Saul's conversion is told three times in Acts (here, 22:3-16, and 26:9-18), with differences in detail. Damascus was a large city with a Jewish community, and the high priest's letters show how far the temple's reach extended among the synagogues. "The Way" is the earliest name for the movement. Jesus' words, "Why do you persecute me?", identify himself with his followers. The Street called Straight was the main east-west road in Damascus and is still partly there. Ananias is called a "disciple" and the word "saints" (hagioi) is used for believers for the first time in Acts. In 2 Corinthians 11:32-33 Paul gives his own account of the escape in a basket, adding that King Aretas' governor was guarding the city; Galatians 1:17-18 adds a stay in Arabia and a three-year gap before Jerusalem, and how to fit the accounts together is debated. Barnabas, whose name means "Son of Encouragement," is the one who vouches for Saul. Tarsus was Saul's home in Cilicia. Lydda was a town on the plain, Sharon a coastal plain, and Joppa a port (modern Jaffa). Dorcas (Greek, "gazelle") is the only woman in the New Testament called a "disciple" (mathētria). A tanner's work with animal skins made him ritually unclean in the eyes of many, so Peter's staying with him foreshadows chapter 10.

questions: Jesus says, "Why do you persecute me?" and not "my followers." What does that identification tell you?
Ananias argues with the Lord about Saul. What do you make of a story in which a follower of Jesus pushes back?
The church is afraid of Saul even after his conversion. How does Barnabas change that?
Tabitha is known by her works of mercy. What does Luke want you to notice about how she is remembered?
